title: Probability as area
objectives: Read a density and find probabilities as areas under it.
Find a CDF and a mean from a density.

screens.title: Chance as area
screens.prose: A trade signal fires at a random time $X$ in the next 4 seconds, later times more likely. The curve describes $X$. The shaded area between the handles $a$ and $b$ is the chance that $X$ lands between them. Drag the handles.
screens.question: Set $a = 2$ and $b = 4$. What is $P(2 \le X \le 4)$?

hints.text: Read the number on the shaded region once the handles sit at 2 and 4.
The whole triangle under the curve has area $\tfrac12 \times 4 \times 0.5 = 1$.
The part left of 2 is a triangle with area $\tfrac12 \times 2 \times 0.25 = 0.25$. The rest is $1 - 0.25$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the handles at 2 and 4 and read the shaded area.

byKey.height: 0.5 is the height of the curve at 4. The chance is the area under the curve, not its height.
byKey.width: 2 is the width of the window. A probability is the area over that window.
byKey.left: 0.25 is the area left of 2. You want the area between 2 and 4.

explain.text: The whole triangle has area 1. The piece left of 2 has area 0.25, so the window from 2 to 4 holds 0.75. For a variable like this, every probability is an area under the curve.

screens.title: A window of width zero
screens.prose: Now squeeze the window around 3. From 2.9 to 3.1 the area is 0.075. Watch it narrow to 2.99 to 3.01.
screens.question: What is $P(X = 3)$, the chance that $X$ is exactly 3?

options.why: You read the height of the curve at 3. A window of width zero holds no area, whatever the height.
That is the window from 2.99 to 3.01. Narrow it further and the area keeps shrinking.
It can: each narrower window around 3 holds less area, and the areas head to 0.

hints.text: What happens to the area each time the window gets 10 times narrower?
Width 0.2 gave 0.075 and width 0.02 gave 0.0075.
The area is about $f(3) \times \text{width}$. A single point has width 0.

feedback.correct: A single point has width 0, so it holds no area.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what area a window of width 0 holds.

byKey.height: You read the height of the curve at 3. A window of width zero holds no area, whatever the height.

explain.text: Width 0.2 held 0.075, about $f(3) \times 0.2$, and width 0.02 held 0.0075. As the width goes to 0, so does the area: $P(X = 3) = 0$. Yet $X$ always takes some value, because the chance lives in intervals, not points.

canvas.caption: Area ≈ f(3) × width, which goes to 0 with the width

screens.title: Total area is 1
screens.prose: A curve read by area like this is a **probability density**, written $f$. $X$ must land somewhere, so the total area under $f$ is 1. Take $f(x) = cx$ on $[0, 4]$ and 0 elsewhere.
screens.question: Slide $c$ until $f$ is a density.

hints.text: Watch the total area as you slide. Which value must it reach?
The shaded triangle has base 4 and height $4c$.
Area $= \tfrac12 \times 4 \times 4c = 8c$. Set $8c = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide until the total area reads 1.000.

byKey.height-one: You made the curve reach height 1 at $x = 4$. The area is then 2. The area must be 1, not the height.

explain.text: The triangle has area $\tfrac12 \times 4 \times 4c = 8c$, so $c = \tfrac18$. That is the density from the first screen, $f(x) = \tfrac{x}{8}$. The rule a density obeys is about area, never about height.

screens.title: The running area
screens.prose: Back to $f(x) = \tfrac{x}{8}$. Drag the handle: the shaded area is $P(X \le x)$, everything up to $x$. As a function of $x$ this is $F(x)$, the **cumulative distribution function**.
screens.question: Write $F(x) = P(X \le x)$ for $0 \le x \le 4$.

hints.text: Try $x = 2$ and $x = 4$. What areas does the canvas show?
The shaded region is a triangle with base $x$ and height $f(x) = \tfrac{x}{8}$.
Area $= \tfrac12 \times x \times \tfrac{x}{8}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the area of the shaded triangle from 0 to $x$.

byKey.density: That is the density, the height at $x$. $F$ is the area up to $x$.
byKey.no-half: You multiplied base by height but left out the half. A triangle's area is $\tfrac12 \times$ base $\times$ height.

explain.text: The triangle up to $x$ has area $\tfrac12 \times x \times \tfrac{x}{8} = \tfrac{x^2}{16}$, the dashed curve. Its slope is $F'(x) = \tfrac{x}{8} = f(x)$: by the fundamental theorem, the density is the derivative of the CDF. So $P(a \le X \le b) = F(b) - F(a)$.

screens.title: The balance point
screens.prose: For a list, $E[X] = \sum x\,P(X = x)$. With a density, a thin strip at $x$ of width $dx$ has chance $f(x)\,dx$. The sum becomes an integral: $E[X] = \int x\,f(x)\,dx$.
screens.question: Find $E[X]$ for $f(x) = \tfrac{x}{8}$ on $[0, 4]$.

hints.text: Multiply $x$ by $\tfrac{x}{8}$, then integrate from 0 to 4.
$\int_0^4 \tfrac{x^2}{8}\,dx = \left[\tfrac{x^3}{24}\right]_0^4$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate $x \cdot \tfrac{x}{8}$ from 0 to 4.

byKey.mid: 2 is the middle of $[0, 4]$. The density puts more weight on later times, so the mean sits above 2.
byKey.second: 8 is $\int_0^4 x^2 f(x)\,dx = E[X^2]$. Weight by $x$, not $x^2$.
byKey.area: 1 is $\int f(x)\,dx$, the total area. Multiply by $x$ before integrating.

explain.text: $\int_0^4 \tfrac{x^2}{8}\,dx = \tfrac{64}{24} = \tfrac83$, right of the midpoint because later times are likelier. In the same way $E[X^2] = \int_0^4 \tfrac{x^3}{8}\,dx = 8$. So $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 8 - \tfrac{64}{9} = \tfrac89$.

screens.title: Taller than 1
screens.prose: An order's fill delay $X$, in seconds, has density $f(x) = 4$ on $[0, 0.25]$ and 0 elsewhere. A colleague objects that a probability cannot be 4.
screens.question: What is $P(0.05 \le X \le 0.1)$?

options.why: You read the height of the density. The chance is the shaded area: width times height.

options.text: None: $f$ is not a density, since $f > 1$
options.why: Height above 1 is allowed. The total area is $4 \times 0.25 = 1$, so $f$ is a density.
You used the width alone. Here the area is width times height, $0.05 \times 4$.

hints.text: Is the colleague reading a height or an area?
The shaded rectangle runs from 0.05 to 0.1.
Width $0.05$, height 4: area $0.05 \times 4$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the area of the shaded rectangle.

byKey.height: You read the height of the density as a probability. The chance is the area: $0.05 \times 4 = 0.2$.
byKey.invalid: Height above 1 is allowed. Only the area must be 1, and here it is: $4 \times 0.25 = 1$.

explain.text: The shaded rectangle has width 0.05 and height 4, so area 0.2. The whole density has area $4 \times 0.25 = 1$, so it is valid even though it reaches 4. A density is chance per unit of $x$: squeeze the range and the height must grow.

screens.title: The rules of a density
screens.prose: Everything you did fits a few lines. A density $f$ has $$f(x) \ge 0, \qquad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1.$$ Probabilities, the CDF and the mean are areas: $$P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a),$$ $$F'(x) = f(x), \qquad E[X] = \int x\,f(x)\,dx.$$
screens.question: Which of these is a density on $[0, 2]$, taken as 0 elsewhere?

options.why: It is negative on $(1, 2]$. A density can never be negative.

hints.text: Check two things: never negative, and area 1.
Find each area on $[0, 2]$.
$\int_0^2 \tfrac{x}{2}\,dx = \left[\tfrac{x^2}{4}\right]_0^2 = 1$.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac{x}{2}$ is never negative on $[0, 2]$ and has area 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each option for area 1 and no negative values.

explain.text: $\int_0^2 \tfrac{x}{2}\,dx = 1$ and $\tfrac{x}{2} \ge 0$ there, so it is a density. Its CDF is $F(x) = \tfrac{x^2}{4}$, whose slope is $\tfrac{x}{2}$ again.

screens.title: Why a point has no chance
screens.prose: You watched $P(X = 3)$ shrink to 0. Now prove $P(X = a) = 0$ for any point $a$, when $f$ stays below some number $M$ near $a$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the proof in order.

lines.text: $P(X = a) \le P(a \le X \le a + h)$ for every $h > 0$, since $a$ lies inside the window
$= \int_a^{a+h} f(x)\,dx$, since a probability is an area
$\le M h$, since the strip fits in a rectangle of height $M$ and width $h$
$Mh \to 0$ as $h \to 0$, and a chance is never negative, so $P(X = a) = 0$

hints.text: Start by trapping the point inside a small window.
Once the window's chance is an integral, bound the integral by a rectangle.
Window, then integral, then rectangle bound, then let $h \to 0$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with the event inside a window, and end with the limit.

byKey.area: The integral is the window's chance, so the window must come first.
byKey.rect: The rectangle bounds the integral, so it follows the integral line.
byKey.limit: Letting $h \to 0$ is the last step: it needs the bound $Mh$ first.

explain.text: The point sits inside every window, so its chance is at most the window's area, which is at most $Mh$. Since $Mh$ can be made as small as we like, $P(X = a) = 0$. So for a density, $P(a \le X \le b)$ and $P(a < X < b)$ are equal.

screens.title: A continuous VaR
screens.prose: A desk's one-day loss $L$, in £m, has density $f(\ell) = \tfrac{10 - \ell}{50}$ on $[0, 10]$. With a list of past losses, the 95% VaR came from the worst 5% of days. Here it is the cut-off whose tail area is 0.05.
screens.question: Find the 95% VaR: the loss $v$ with $P(L > v) = 0.05$. Give $v$ to 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Drag the handle until the tail area reads 0.050.
The tail is a triangle: width $10 - v$, height $\tfrac{10 - v}{50}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the tail area to 0.05 and solve for $v$.

byKey.width: You went 95% of the way along the axis. The tail must hold 5% of the area, not 5% of the width.
byKey.gap: $\sqrt5 \approx 2.24$ is the tail's width $10 - v$. Subtract it from 10.
byKey.half: Beyond 5 the area is $\tfrac{25}{100} = 0.25$, far more than 0.05. Move further right.

explain.text: $\tfrac{(10 - v)^2}{100} = 0.05$ gives $v = 10 - \sqrt5 \approx 7.76$. The desk loses more than £7.76m on about 1 day in 20. A discrete VaR counts the worst days; a continuous one solves for a tail area.

screens.title: An option's expected payoff
screens.prose: Tomorrow's price $S$ has a triangular density: $p(s) = \tfrac{s - 90}{100}$ on $[90, 100]$ and $\tfrac{110 - s}{100}$ on $[100, 110]$. A call struck at £105 pays $\max(S - 105, 0)$.
screens.question: What is the expected payoff $\int \max(s - 105, 0)\,p(s)\,ds$, in pounds? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Below £105 the payoff is 0, so integrate from 105 to 110 only.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate $(s - 105)\,p(s)$ from 105 to 110.

byKey.at-mean: You put the mean price, £100, into the payoff. The average of the payoff is not the payoff at the average.
byKey.max-times-p: You multiplied the largest payoff, £5, by $P(S > 105)$. Most paths above 105 pay much less than £5.
byKey.prob: 0.125 is $P(S > 105)$, the chance the call pays at all. Weight each payoff by its density.
byKey.strike-100: That is the call struck at £100. This one is struck at £105.

explain.text: $\tfrac{1}{100}\left(62.5 - \tfrac{125}{3}\right) = \tfrac{125}{600} \approx$ £0.21. The payoff at the mean price is 0, which ignores every path above 105. An expected payoff is an integral of payoff times density, just as $E[X]$ is.

ideas: A density $f$ gives probabilities as areas: $P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$. A single point has width 0, so $P(X = a) = 0$.
$f \ge 0$ and its total area is 1. Its height can exceed 1; height is chance per unit, not chance.
The CDF is the running area, $F(x) = P(X \le x)$, and $F' = f$. The mean is $E[X] = \int x\,f(x)\,dx$.

formula.name: Probability as area
formula.tex: P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)
formula.note: Total area 1; the endpoints make no difference.

summary.trap: The height $f(x)$ is not a probability. $P(X = 3)$ is 0, not $f(3)$, and a density may rise above 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate $3x^2$ from 0 to 0.5.

byKey.height: 0.75 is the height $f(0.5)$. The chance is the area up to 0.5.
byKey.width: 0.5 is the width of the window, not the area over it.

explain.text: $\int_0^{0.5} 3x^2\,dx = \left[x^3\right]_0^{0.5} = 0.125$. The density is small near 0, so most of the chance sits near 1.

options.why: You integrated $F$. The density is the derivative of the CDF.
That is the CDF itself, the running area. The density is its slope.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Differentiate the CDF.

explain.text: The CDF is the running area, so its slope is the density: $f(x) = F'(x) = 3x^2$. Check: $\int_0^1 3x^2\,dx = 1$.

options.why: You read the height as a probability. A single point holds no area.
Its area is $2 \times 0.5 = 1$. A density may rise above 1.
0.5 is $P(X \le 0.25)$, an interval. The single point has chance 0.

feedback.correct: A point has chance 0, and the area up to 0.25 is $2 \times 0.25 = 0.5$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate points, which hold no area, from intervals.

explain.text: A single point has width 0, so $P(X = 0.25) = 0$. The interval $[0, 0.25]$ has area $2 \times 0.25 = 0.5$. The density is valid: total area $2 \times 0.5 = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $E[X^2] = \int_0^1 x^2 \cdot 2x\,dx$ first.

byKey.mean-not-sq: You used $E[X] - E[X]^2$. The first term is $E[X^2] = \int x^2 f(x)\,dx = \tfrac12$.
